Efficient Treatment and Simultaneous Energy Recovery from Cattle
Wastewater by the Micro-Aerated UASB and SBR Coupled System

ABSTRACT: The present study introduces a coupled system comprising
an upflow anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB) and a sequencing batch
reactor (SBR) to treat intensive cattle farming wastewater. The results
confirmed that the optimal conditions for UASB were an organic load rate
of 9.98 kg-COD m−3·day−1, a C/N ratio of 22, and a hydraulic retention
time (HRT) of 1.5 h. For the SBR reactor, the optimal conditions are a
dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration of 6.08 mg L−1 and the S2 aeration
mode. Under these optimal conditions, the study achieved anaerobic and
aerobic sludge granules (0.25−0.5 and 0.5−0.75 mm) with excellent
properties due to the cooperation of a functional microbial community,
including Synergistetes, Thermotogae, Acidobacteria, Proteobacteria, Chloro-
flexi, and Hyd24−12 in UASB and Paracoccus, Proteobacteria, Chloroflexi,
and Acinetobacter in SBR. This hybrid system contributed 94% of chemical
oxygen demand (COD), 90% of NH4
+-N, 90% of TN, and 61% of TP.
Additionally, it achieved 18% net energy recovery from the real cattle wastewater, indicating that the UASB−SBR-coupled system
holds potential as an approach for treating and recovering energy from cattle wastewater.
KEYWORDS: cattle wastewater, UASB−SBR-coupled system, anaerobic/aerobic activated sludge granulation, microbial community,
energy balance
■INTRODUCTION
Intensive cattle farming has increasingly been adopted
worldwide, resulting in the generation of substantial amounts
of wastewater.1 This wastewater can reach up to 130 L per
animal per day and contains high concentrations of pollutants,
including BOD5 ranging from 2000 to 30,000 mg L−1, total
nitrogen ranging from 200 to 2055 mg L−1, ammonia between
110 and 1650 mg L−1, total phosphorus varying from 100 to
620 mg L−1, and suspended solid 200−1200 mg L−1.2
Uncontrolled discharge of the concentrate contaminants can
cause DO depletion in water courses, eutrophication, ground-
water contamination, and air pollution by ammonia volatiliza-
tion.3,4 Consequently, cattle wastewater has become an
emerging environmental concern and more robust treatment
techniques are required to meet increasingly stringent
environmental standards in cattle farming.
Due to the slow degradation of complex pollutants and high
nitrogen and phosphorus levels, as well as the occurrence of
hydraulic and organic shock loads, specific technology is
required to treat cattle wastewater.5 A coupled system of up-
flow anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB) and sequencing batch
reactor (SBR) with aerobic granular sludge (AGS) has the
potential to efficiently treat cattle wastewater. Compared to
conventional treatment systems, granular sludge systems have
lower reactor volume requirements and lower sludge handling
costs while also exhibiting high removal efficiencies of organic
matter, nitrogen, and phosphorous.6 This system is capable of
recovering energy from wastewater through biogas production,
while simultaneously achieving the removal of organic
pollutants and meeting the nitrogen and phosphorus
concentration requirements for effluent from the aerobic
stage in accordance with surface water discharge standards.7−9
However, there are some obstacles that hinder the
widespread use of the hybrid UASB and SBR system, such
as a long start-up period, low stability, and disintegration.10,11
In order to effectively capture a majority of the organic matter
within a short retention time in the UASB, micro-aeration is
employed, which accelerates the hydrolysis of organics (the
rate-limiting step of the anaerobic process).12,13 Proper micro-
aeration in the UASB system does not hinder the formation of
anaerobic granular sludge (AnGS).14 On the other hand, the

SBR system presents high potential for nitrogen and
phosphorus removal. However, its performance depends on
the dissolved oxygen (DO) level since a low DO level cannot
assist the formation of activated granular sludge (AGS),15
while excessive DO can not only affect microbial growth but
also be detrimental to energy consumption and phosphorus
removal.16
To date, the integration of two different granular sludge
systems for the efficient removal of high-concentration
pollutants has been rarely reported and the conditions for
the rapid cultivation of AnGS and AGS have not been
disclosed yet. The objective of this study is to explore the
proper conditions for rapid granulation of AnGS and AGS to
remove pollutants in cattle wastewater. To achieve this goal,
two identical UASB reactors with and without micro-aeration
are constructed and operated under similar conditions for
comparison. The SBR reactor is also optimized by altering the
DO concentration and aeration mode. By analyzing the
differences in sludge properties, nutrient removal, and
microbial communities, we reveal the relevant mechanism of
intensive cattle farming wastewater treatment via the hybrid
system of UASB and SBR. By addressing real wastewater
samples, this study provides valuable insights into the practical
application and effectiveness of the combined granular sludge
system in the removal of high-concentration pollutants.
■METHODS AND MATERIALS
UASB−SBR Configuration. The schematic diagram in
Figure 1 illustrates the flow of the test device. Two UASB
reactors, each with a water jacket and a three-phase separation
zone, were constructed from acrylic material. The entire
reactor had a working volume of 7.5 L and was divided into
three sections: the bottom section had an inner diameter of 80
mm and a height of 7.52 cm, the middle section had an inner
diameter of 160 mm and a height of 40 mm, and the top
section had an inner diameter of 160 mm and a height of 210
mm. The SBR, also made of acrylic, had a working volume of
4.27 L, with a height of 1000 mm and an inner diameter of 80
mm. The reactor’s top was fitted with an electric stirrer, pH,
and DO monitors, while the bottom had a rubber aeration
plate connected to an air pump and a gas-flow meter. To adjust
the hydraulic retention time and for sampling analysis, a
sampling port was installed every 10 cm along the reactor’s
exterior. The reactor effluent pipe was connected to a solenoid
valve controlled by a programmable controller.
Start-up and Operation. To initiate the experiment, we
inoculated 10.0 g L−1 of anaerobic sludge and 3.2 g L−1 of
aerobic sludge into the UASB and SBR, respectively. Both
sludges were collected from the Chengnan wastewater
treatment plant in Chongqing, China. We cultivated and
optimized the UASB and SBR independently using synthetic
wastewater to achieve the best possible performance. We then
conducted two different experiments on the UASBs. In the first
experiment, we aerated one of the UASB reactors with DO
levels around 1 mg L−1 at the top to stimulate bacterial growth,
as the DO level in the reaction zone was low. In the second
experiment, we operated another UASB in strict anaerobic
conditions for 120 days (phase I).
The SBR was cultivated with two aeration modes: S1 (5 min
inlet →320 min aeration →30 min sedimentation →5 min
drainage) and S2 (5 min inlet →90 min aeration →60 min
aeration- suspending →60 min aeration →75 min aeration-
suspending⃗45 min aeration →30 min sedimentation →5 min
drainage). Before treating real cattle wastewater, we optimized
both the UASB and SBR. The influent COD concentration of
the UASB fluctuated irregularly between 3000 and 15,000 mg
L−1, with an organic load ranging between 2.366 and 12.326 kg
COD m−3 day−1. We controlled the upper DO level at about 1
mg L−1, and the C/N ratios were 25:1, 22:1, 20:1, 18:1, 15:1,
and 10:1. The HRTs were 12, 20, 24, 36, and 48 h,
respectively. The DO concentrations of the SBR were 3.10,
4.12, 5.19, 6.08, 7.11, and 8.01 mg L−1, respectively. After
reaching the optimal state, we combined the UASB and SBR

Chemical Analysis and Sludge Characterization.
Standard measurements were used to analyze COD, nitrogen
(NH4
+-N, NO3
−-N, NO2
N, and TN), phosphorus (TP), and
other items. The appearance of AGS under different conditions
was characterized using a scanning electron microscope (SEM)
from Hitachi Ltd., Japan (model: SU8020). Particle size was
measured using a laser densitometer from Malvern Panalytical
Ltd., Shanghai, China (model: Mastersizer 3000).
Energy Balance Analysis. Energy balance is presented
with the energy balance ratio (EBR), which is the ratio of
energy recovery converted from biogas produced by COD to
energy consumption by the heater, aeration, and pumps in the
throughput system.17
Microbial Community Structural Analysis. To analyze
microbial samples, multiple portions of biofilms were collected
using aseptic scissors under different conditions. Each
condition was subjected to five repeated fed-batch cycles
before the biofilm samples were collected. The microbial
samples from the UASB (upflow anaerobic sludge blanket)
reactor were designated as UASBi (inoculated activated
sludge), UASB1 (anaerobic activated sludge in a stable
state), UASB2 (anaerobic activated sludge under optimal
conditions), and UASB3 (anaerobic activated sludge from real
livestock wastewater). Similarly, the microbial samples from
the SBR were named SBRi, SBR1, SBR2, and SBR3. Genomic
DNA was extracted from the samples using the DNeasy
PowerSoil Kit (Qiagen, Inc., Netherlands), as described in our
published paper.11 The pair of primers 338f (5′-ACT CCT
ACG GGA GGC AGC A-3′) and 806r (5′-TCG GAC TAC
HVG GGT WTC TAA T-3′) targeted the V3−V4 regions of
the 16S rRNA genes, which were selected for polymerase chain
reactions of amplicon library preparation.18 Finally, the
amplicons were sequenced using the Illumina MiSeq platform.
A total of 886,145 nucleotide sequence reads from eight
samples were analyzed using QIIME 2.19 The DADA2
algorithm was utilized for denoising, resulting in 417,278
high-quality paired-end reads with an average length of 251
bp.20 These filtered reads were then clustered into 4183
amplicon sequence variants (ASVs), and taxonomy was
assigned to them utilizing the Greengenes Databases
(V13_8). Furthermore, a phylogenetic tree was generated
using ARB software.21 To predict the functional gene
abundance, picrust2 was used based on the microbial
community structure reflected by 16S rRNA gene sequencing
data.22 Moreover, canonical correspondence analysis (CCA)
was conducted using the VEGAN package (V2.6-2) in R
(version 4.0.3), based on the microbial community structure of
genus level and the operation condition of the reactors.
■RESULTS
UASB Performance. The performances of single UASB,
SBR, and integrated UASB−SBR were discussed according to
the removal efficiencies of COD, NH4
+, TN, and TP. The
operating period was divided into three phases: phase I (0−

120 days, cultivation period); phase II (121−180 days),
optimization period; and phase III (181−220 days, real cattle
wastewater fed), as displayed in Figure 2.
To investigate the effect of micro-aeration in UASB, two
parallel UASB reactors were operated simultaneously. One of
the reactors was equipped with top aeration, allowing a trace
amount of DO in the reaction zone to simulate the effect of
micro-aeration. The other reactor was operated under strictly
anaerobic conditions. Initially, the COD removal efficiency of
the UASB with micro-aeration was low and unstable (1−20
days, Figure 2a) due to the continuous washing out of sludge
from the reactor (Supporting Information: Figure S1) resulting
from the intake without anaerobic precipitation. Over the next
50 days, the anaerobic activated sludge in the UASB gradually
transformed from loose flocs to small particles.
As the intake COD concentration rose from 3000 to 8000
mg L−1, COD removal rates increased to 95% (micro-aeration)
and 96% (strictly anaerobic). However, when the COD intake
increased to 16,000 mg L−1, the COD removal rates in both
UASB reactors decreased to around 92% due to the occurrence
of acidified influent inside the reactor, which inhibited the
activity of methanogenic bacteria. This phenomenon indicates
that excessive organic load negatively affects the role of
microorganisms in COD removal. Despite the formation of
AnGS in both reactors, the effluent COD concentrations were
almost the same, when the sludge load was not too high, and
the AnGS was adaptable.
When considering nitrogen removal in UASB reactors, we
measured four parameters: NH4
+-N, NO3
−-N, NO2
−-N, and
TN. Initially, during the adaptation period, the concentration
of NH4
+-N remained relatively stable for the first 20 days as the
anaerobic activated sludge was inactivated. However, as the
anaerobic bacteria gradually adapted to the environment,
differences between the two UASB reactors became more
pronounced. Over the following 40 days, the NH4
+-N removal
rates increased to 70% in the top-aeration UASB and 30% in
the strictly anaerobic UASB, respectively. Eventually, both
UASB reactors reached a stable state by the 120th day, as
depicted in Figure 2b.
Analyzing the nitrogen variations throughout the complete
cycle, it was evident that the UASB system with top micro-
aeration exhibited an impressive TN removal rate of 90%, with
minimal accumulation of no more than 1% NO3
−-N and
negligible levels of NO2
−-N. In contrast, the strictly anaerobic
UASB achieved 75% of TN removal, including the
accumulation of 23% NO3
−-N and 2% NO2
−-N (Supporting
Information: Figure S2). These differences can be attributed to
the fact that the top-aeration UASB reactor created a low DO
condition, promoting the synergistic activity of facultative
anaerobic, anaerobic, and aerobic bacteria, which led to higher
nitrogen removal rates.
Regarding TP removal, both reactors experienced a
fluctuating increase within the first 80 days and reached a
relatively stable status of 40% removal by the 120th day. The
top-aeration reactor exhibited a higher TP removal rate, which
can be attributed to the enhanced biological activity facilitated
by micro-aeration in the UASB reactor. The introduction of a
low level of DO through micro-aeration promoted the activity
of aerobic bacteria, which utilize oxygen for their metabolic
processes. These aerobic bacteria played a crucial role in the
bioconversion of phosphorus, resulting in higher phosphorus
removal rates. Micro-aeration also fostered the growth of a
diverse microbial community within the UASB reactor,
comprising not only anaerobic bacteria but also facultative
anaerobic and aerobic bacteria. The coexistence of these
microbial groups created a synergistic effect, where their
combined activities contributed to more efficient phosphorus
removal. Additionally, the presence of oxygen in the micro-
aerated UASB reactor facilitated the uptake of phosphorus by
microorganisms, particularly aerobic bacteria, which have a
higher affinity for phosphorus and can accumulate it within
their cells. Consequently, the overall phosphorus removal
efficiency of the system is enhanced. Furthermore, micro-
aeration positively influenced the settling properties of the
sludge in the UASB reactor. The presence of oxygen promoted
the formation of denser and better-settling sludge flocs,
improving settling characteristics and preventing the washout
of biomass from the reactor. This ensured the retention of
phosphorus-accumulating bacteria, further enhancing phos-
phorus removal efficiency.
The UASB reactor was optimized by adjusting the C/N
ratios and HRT. Specifically, as the C/N ratio gradually
decreased from 25:1 to 10:1, there was a slight drop in COD
removal rate from 92 to 90%. However, when the HRT was
extended from 12 to 48 h, the COD removal rate slightly
increased from 92 to 94.5%. The COD trend indicates that the
C/N ratio and HRT are not the sole limiting factors for simple
substrates (Supporting Information: Figure S3). Following the
optimization of the C/N ratio and HRT, the removal rates of
NH4
+, TN, and TP were recovered at 75, 99, and 60%,
respectively (phase II in Figure 2). Therefore, a single UASB
reactor can effectively remove organic matter but a part of
nitrogen and phosphorus.
SBR Performance. The single SBR reactor experienced an
adaption period (0−20 days) of which the removal rates of
COD, NH4
+-N, TN, and TP were relatively low. Then, the
removal rates of these three parameters increased to 75, 60,
and 20% on the 20th day, respectively, and continuously
climbed and reached a stable status (88% COD, 75% TN, and
30% TP) on the 120th day, with a DO concentration of 3.0 mg
L−1 (phase I).
SBR was further optimized by varying the DO levels at 3, 4,
5, 6, 7, and 8 mg L−1. The removal rate of COD increased to
95% when the DO level was enhanced to 6.0 mg L−1.
However, there was no further increase in the removal rate
even when the DO level was increased to 8.0 mg L−1
(Supporting Information: Figure S4). This trend indicates
that the optimal DO level for the SBR is 6.0 mg L−1 and
increasing the DO level beyond that does not provide
additional benefits. At a DO level of 6.0 mg L−1, the SBR
was optimized by varying the reaction times at 6, 8, 12, and 24
h. Only slight increases in the removal rates of COD were
observed with an extended reaction time from 6 to 24 h, as
shown in the additional figure (Supporting Information: Figure
S4). This suggests that reaction time is not a crucial factor
affecting pollutant removal and extending the reaction time
consumes more energy. Under the conditions of a DO level of
6.0 mg L−1 and a reaction time of 6 h, the SBR reactor was
operated with two aeration modes, S1 and S2. The results
indicate that the removal rates of COD and NH4
+-N for S1
and S2 modes were not significantly different but the removal
rates of TN and TP for S2 mode increased by 19 and 10.0%,
respectively. These increases in the removal rates of TN and
TP can be attributed to the alternating anaerobic and aerobic
operation mode, which meets the requirements of enriching
ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) and inhibiting nitrite-

Real Cattle Wastewater Feeding. In phase III, real cattle
wastewater was diluted with synthetic wastewater at varying
ratios of 20, 40, 60, 80, and 100% to mitigate the impact of
concentrated pollutants. The UASB−SBR-integrated system
was able to remove approximately 97% of COD, 95% of NH4
+-
N, 73% of TN, and 80% of TP when real cattle wastewater was
at a concentration of 20%. As the proportion of real cattle
wastewater increased to 100%, the rate of COD removal
slightly decreased to 95% while the rate of NH4

10%.
In addition, the use of intermittent aeration in the AGS
process improved nitrogen removal efficiency, despite
variations in objectives and conditions compared to the
present study. Concentration profiles demonstrated the
favorable impact of intermittent aeration on nitrogen removal,
consistent with other studies.24 These excellent results were
attributed to the positive properties of the anaerobic/aerobic
activated sludge and the functional microorganism community,
as elaborated in the next section.
Anaerobic/Aerobic Activate Sludge Properties. Figure
3 illustrates the characteristics and particle distributions of
anaerobic/aerobic activated sludge collected under different
conditions. Initially, the inoculated sludge was composed of
fine flocculent sludge, wherein the low activity and MLSS of
the microorganisms prevented them from aggregating to form
granular sludge. Subsequently, the flocculent-activated sludge
grew with good settling performance and formed small
particles with compact structures and regular shapes due to
the interaction between microorganisms and hydraulic shear
force. At the stable status (Figure 3a), AnGS particles became
granules with diameters of about 1.0−1.5 mm, which were
much larger than those observed in our previous study without
micro-aeration.11 Micro-aeration thus facilitated the self-
agglomeration of microorganisms.
SEM was used to further characterize the morphological
structures of mature AnGS. At a magnification of ×1000, the
microscopic colonies consisted mainly of cocci and bacilli,
interspersed with short filamentous bacteria. The long bacilli
formed pore spaces on the surface inside the particles, which
was important for biofilm formation and cell attachment to

The characteristics of AGS are shown in the lower part of

Compared to the aerobic granules cultivated with S1 aeration

Microbiological Community and Structure in UASB.
The microbiological composition of the UASB reactor was
analyzed, and the top 30 genera in relative abundance are
shown in Figure 4a. These genera belonged to nine phyla,
namely, Firmicutes, Synergistetes, Thermotogae, Acidobacteria,
Proteobacteria, Chloroflexi, Chlorobi, Bacteroidetes, and Hyd24-
12. It was observed that the microbial community structure in
the UASB reactor was significantly different from that of the
inoculated sludge (UASB1).
During the initial stage, the most predominant genus
(UASBi) was Acinetobacter, which belonged to Proteobacteria
and has a relative abundance of 46.52%. Acinetobacter is a
group of non-fermentative aerobic bacteria that are widely
distributed in wastewater treatment systems. They have the
capability to degrade non-glucose carbon sources, such as
short-chain fatty acids, phenol, and alcohol.26 Other genera
that had comparatively high relative abundance included
Brachymonas (7.91%) and Diaphorobacter (5.09%) from
Proteobacteria, Macellibacteroides (4.06%) from Bacteroidetes,
and Chlorobiaceae (7.87%) from Chlorobi. All of these genera
can ferment carbohydrates into diverse organic acids.27
Brachymonas bacteria serve a structural function and contribute
to the formation of sludge granules in wastewater treatment
systems.28 Brachymonas and Diaphorobacter have also been
reported as denitrifying bacteria in granular sludge.29,30
Macellibacteroides plays a significant role in polymer degrada-
tion and the production of volatile fatty acids (VFAs).31
Furthermore, Chlorobiaceae has been identified as green sulfur
bacteria that utilize sulfur, sulfide, and thiosulfate as electron
donors.32
In phase II, the abundance of Proteobacteria in the granular
sludge (UASB2) decreased and was replaced mainly by
microorganisms from Firmicutes, Synergistetes, and Bacteroidetes.
Among these phyla, the highest abundance was found in
ML635J-40 (12.87%) and Bacteroidales (11.92%) from
Bacteroidetes, Syntrophomonas (11.05%), and Clostridiales
(8.09%) from Firmicutes. Bacteroidetes, represented by
Bacteroidales, exhibit saccharolytic and proteolytic activity in
anaerobic systems, while some short-chain fatty acids such as
propionate, acetate, and succinate are produced.33 Clostridiales
mainly hydrolyze and ferment carbohydrates.34 Bacteria in
Syntrophomonas degrade long-chain fatty acids via β-
oxidation.35 Members of the Synergistetes phylum play a
prominent role in protein and amino acid degradation.36
Meanwhile, Clostridiales and Syntrophomonas utilize short-
chain fatty acids through syntrophic metabolism with
methanogens and supply hydrogen and acetic acid for methane
production.37
When real wastewater (UASB3) was introduced to the
UASB reactor (phase III), the abundance of bacteria in several
phyla, including Synergistetes, Thermotogae, Acidobacteria,
Proteobacteria, Chloroflexi, and Hyd24-12, significantly in-
creased. Conversely, the bacterial abundance of Bacteroidetes
and Firmicutes decreased. Notably, the increase in sulfur-
reducing bacteria such as Unclassified ASSO-13 (6.71%) and
Desulfovibrio (1.92%) from Proteobacteria, as well as
Acinetobacter (2.06%) from Acidobacteria, may be linked to
the presence of sulfur-containing proteins in the real poultry
wastewater.38 Moreover, the abundance of Synergistetes, a
group of protein-metabolizing bacteria, also increased. Other
microorganisms showed an increase due to the presence of
complex organic matter and other substances in the real
poultry wastewater. The Anaerolineae group (Unclassified
GCA004, 3.60%; Unclassified SHA-31, 3.27%; and Unclassified
Chlorobiaceae, 0.02%), known as fatty acid-oxidizing syntrophs
in the processes,39 showed an increase. Kosmotoga (3.82%) was
also reported to be associated with the degradation of some
complex organic compounds.40
Microbiological Community and Structure in SBR. In

■CONCLUSIONS
This study developed a coupled system consisting of top-aired
UASB and SBR to simultaneously recover biogas and remove
nutrients from cattle wastewater. Prior to the coupling of
UASB and SBR, each component was independently
optimized. The results demonstrated that UASB operated
with top micro-aeration had larger AnGS particles compared to
that operated under strict anaerobic conditions. Similarly, the
SBR operated with S2 aeration mode produced larger AGS
particles with round shapes and smooth surfaces when
compared to the control group (S1). Under the optimal
conditions, this hybrid system contributed 94% of COD, 90%
of NH4
+-N, 90% TN, and 61% of PO4
3-P removed from real
cattle wastewater, with the cooperation of Synergistetes,
Thermotogae, Acidobacteria, Proteobacteria, Chloroflexi, and
Hyd24-12 dominated in UASB, and Paracoccus, Proteobacteria,
Chloroflexi, and Acinetobacter. The energy balance analysis
revealed that the generated biogas accounted for 18% of the
net energy. These findings highlight the potential of the
UASB−SBR-coupled system as an effective approach for
energy recovery from cattle wastewater.
